title: Sentence Foundations: See the Pattern
description: Begin noticing how a Hawaiian sentence is organized without forcing English word order onto it.

sourceReview.notes: The Hawaiian example is taken from UH Maui College's E Hoʻoulu Lāhui Pepeke Painu instructional page. The learner-facing breakdown uses plain-English labels and does not introduce broader conversational claims beyond the sourced example.

activities.instruction: See how the sentence is built.
activities.prompt: Start with the pattern, not an English word-for-word translation.
activities.support: This first sentence lesson is for understanding. There is nothing to memorize or pass yet.
activities.sentence: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.patternIntro: In this example, the action comes first, followed by who is doing it, then what the action is directed toward.

parts.label: Action
parts.note: The sentence begins with the action: eat/eats.

parts.label: Who
parts.note: This part identifies Lani as the person doing the action.

parts.label: What
parts.note: This part tells what Lani eats: the poi.

activities.languageNote: Hawaiian does not need to mirror English word order. For now, notice the shape of this sentence and let the pattern become familiar.
